newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian army expects wage payments in two months.
newsitem.headline: Russian army expects wage payments in two months.

text.p: The Russian army's chief financial officer said on Thursday he was sure the government would meet its target of ending wage arrears to the military in two months.
But Lieutenant-General Georgy Oleinik, head of the armed forces main directorate for budget and finance, said the financial situation in the army remained bad.

President Boris Yeltsin, who has ordered military reforms, told the government this week to settle the military wage debt in the next two months. Oleinik said the arrears totalled 8.1 trillion roubles ($1.4 billion).
"If this debt is wiped out, and I am sure it will be, then our servicemen will receive their wage arrears by September 1 -- in the time planned," Oleinik told a news conference.

He said servicemen in remote and difficult areas such as northern Russia and the Far East would receive their money first, then soldiers on active combat and then the military in other, less demanding areas.
Government officials have put the backlog of wages to the armed forces at closer to five trillion roubles ($860 million).

Oleinik said the military were not receiving all the funds due to them in the budget, although the 88.3 trillion roubles ($15.3 billion) initially set aside for the armed forces had been reduced to 67.2 trillion ($11.6 billion) under budget cuts.
"I want to draw your attention to the fact that half a year has already passed and we have received so far only 33 percent of what was provided for in the reduced budget," he said.
"The state of financing in the armed forces remains extremely difficult...You understand that reform of the armed forces is only possible if financing issues are addressed."
Oleinik said the government would also gradually settle other debts to servicemen, including unpaid child and food allowances.
"In September and October and further on, in any case by the end of the year, all these (other) arrears will be paid," he said.
The armed forces were once Moscow's pride and joy but have fallen on hard times since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
Some soldiers have not been paid for months, morale is low and the armed forces were humiliated in a nearly 21-month war with Chechen separatists which ended last August.

Yeltsin plans to reduce manpower in the armed forces from about 1.5 million to 1.2 million next year. Oleinik said he believed the optimum number of servicemen on current spending levels would be 900,000.
